screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear distinction: functional requirements describe what the system does — the visible behaviors and features. For example, "users can upload photos" is a functional statement. Non-functional requirements describe how well the system performs those behaviors; they are about quality attributes. An NFR could be "uploads must complete within two seconds for 95 percent of users," which constrains architecture, testing, and cost. This distinction matters because architects often select different components and trade-offs depending on quality goals. A web app that must simply store photos will emphasize correctness and durability. A photo-sharing service with millions of users must prioritize scalability and throughput. A common misconception is to think of NFRs as secondary or optional; in practice they are first-class requirements because they determine whether a feature is usable. A second misconception is treating NFRs as binary: they are measurable and continuous, so convert them into percentiles or rates. A concrete interview-ready script: name the requirement, classify it as functional or non-functional, and state its acceptance criterion. For practice, take any feature and write both a functional sentence and a measurable NFR for it. That habit forces you to design with testable goals and clear constraints.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Functional = what. Non-functional = how well. Always quantify NFRs so they are actionable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Functional vs Non-Functional
Definition and contrast
A direct comparison to form the habit of classifying requirements correctly.
Functional requirement
Describes system behavior. Example: users can upload photos. Acceptance: upload finishes without error.
Non-Functional requirement
Describes quality of behavior. Example: uploads under 2 seconds for 95% of requests. Acceptance: measurable latency SLO.
Common mistakes
  • Treating NFRs as optional instead of primary constraints.
  • Leaving them vague: avoid "fast" or "reliable" without a metric.
Key Takeaway

Always pair a functional statement with at least one measurable non-functional target.

Concrete examples to practice
Convert these features into functional + NFR pairs.
Feature: Search
Functional: return matching items for a query. NFR: 90% of searches return first page within 150 ms.
Feature: Payment processing
Functional: process a payment and return a confirmation. NFR: transaction durability must guarantee no data loss on commit.
Practice prompt
Pick a feature from an app you know and write both a functional requirement and a measurable NFR. Use percentiles and units to make it testable.

screens.title: Scalability: Vertical vs Horizontal
screens.narratorSegment: Scalability is the system’s ability to handle increasing work by adding resources. Two common approaches are vertical scaling and horizontal scaling. Vertical scaling means making a single machine more powerful — more C P U, R A M, or disk. It’s straightforward and often cheapest early on, but it hits hard limits and creates a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads load across them. It offers higher capacity and fault tolerance, but introduces distributed complexity: state management, data partitioning, coordination, and potential consistency issues. In practice, many systems start vertical and adopt horizontal strategies as load grows. A concrete example: a small photo app might move from a beefy single database instance to a sharded cluster with read replicas as user counts rise. A common misconception is that horizontal scaling is always the better option; it often is for very large systems, but if your traffic is small, horizontal complexity is costly and unnecessary. When you choose horizontal scaling, quantify targets: number of requests per second, expected nodes, and acceptable coordination overhead. That quantification helps choose between stateless horizontal web servers, partitioned databases, or managed services that offload operational complexity.

keyIdea.title: Scalability Trade
keyIdea.text: Scale up for early simplicity; scale out for capacity and resilience, but plan for distributed state and consistency.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Scalability
Vertical scaling (Scale Up)
Add resources to a single server: CPUs, memory, or disk.
When to use
Early stages, small traffic, simpler operational needs.
Limits
Hardware ceilings, single point of failure, cost at scale.
Example

A prototype with one database instance upgraded from 4 to 32 cores to meet a 10x traffic spike temporarily.

Horizontal scaling (Scale Out)
Add more machines and distribute work across them.
When to use
Large, global systems that must serve many concurrent users reliably.
Costs
Increased system complexity: partitioning, distributed coordination, and consistency management.
Key Takeaway

Choose scale strategy based on traffic forecasts and operational tolerance for distributed complexity.

screens.title: Availability and Reliability
screens.narratorSegment: Availability measures the proportion of time a system is accessible, usually expressed in 'nines' like 99.9% or 99.999%. Higher availability requires redundancy, automated failover, and disaster recovery plans. Reliability relates to the probability a system performs correctly over time; it captures fault tolerance and the ability to operate despite component failures. These two are related but distinct: a system can be highly available yet unreliable if it often returns incorrect or stale results. Achieving high availability often implies running redundant components across failure domains and automating detection and recovery. For reliability, design for graceful degradation and correctness under partial failures. A practical example: to achieve three nines, you might run services across two availability zones with automatic health checks and rolling restarts; to reach five nines you introduce cross-region replication and rigorous incident runbooks. A frequent misconception is equating uptime with correctness. For interviews, be prepared to propose redundancy patterns, explain failover behavior, and show how data correctness is preserved during recovery. Always quantify the target number of nines and the recovery time objective so your architectural choices can be validated.

keyIdea.text: Availability is measurable uptime; reliability is the probability of correct operation over time — both require different design techniques.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Availability & Reliability
Availability
Proportion of time a system is operational; expressed as nines.
Measurement
Percent uptime per year: e.g., 99.9% ≈ 8.76 hours downtime/year.
Techniques
Redundancy, health checks, failover, multi-zone or multi-region deployments.
Example

Use read replicas and automated failover to maintain 99.95% availability during maintenance windows.

Reliability
Probability the system functions correctly over time; emphasizes correctness under failures.
Measurement
Mean time between failures, error rates, and correctness checks over a period.
Techniques
Idempotent operations, retry logic, data validation, and consistent recovery paths.
Common pitfall

High availability without correctness can still harm users if data is frequently inconsistent or lost.

screens.title: Latency vs Throughput
screens.narratorSegment: Latency and throughput describe two different performance aspects. Latency is the time delay between a single request and its response. Low latency is critical for real-time experiences like online gaming or interactive search. Throughput measures the number of operations a system can process per unit of time, such as requests per second. A streaming service needs high throughput to serve many concurrent users. The relationship between the two can be subtle: you can have low latency for a few requests but low throughput overall, or high throughput with longer individual latencies when the system is saturated. Optimization strategies differ: to lower latency you can cache responses, optimize hot code paths, or move compute closer to the user. To increase throughput you scale horizontally, partition work, or use asynchronous processing. A frequent misconception is optimizing one while ignoring the other — for example, adding aggressive caching might reduce latency but increase staleness, impacting correctness. When designing, quantify targets like '95 percent of requests under 100 milliseconds' and 'system must sustain 10,000 requests per second' so that both dimensions are addressed with appropriate mechanisms.

keyIdea.title: Performance Measures
keyIdea.text: Latency is per-request delay; throughput is operations per time. Both must be quantified and optimized with complementary techniques.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Latency & Throughput
Latency
Time between request and response — experienced per user.
Quantify
Use percentiles: e.g., 95th percentile under 100 ms.
Techniques
Caching, CDN, edge compute, and faster data paths.
Throughput
How many operations a system completes per time unit.
Quantify
Requests per second, transactions per minute, or concurrent streams.
Techniques
Horizontal scaling, batching, and asynchronous processing.
Concrete example
A streaming API might require sub-200 ms latency for interactive controls while supporting 50,000 concurrent streams. Design choices must balance both targets: edge caching for latency and partitioned stream processors for throughput.

screens.title: Durability and Data Guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: Durability is the guarantee that once data is committed it will persist and not be lost, even when components fail. This is essential for databases, payment systems, and any system where loss of committed writes is unacceptable. Techniques that improve durability include write-ahead logs, synchronous replication to multiple durable stores, and stable commit protocols. There is often a cost trade-off: synchronous replication across regions increases latency and cost but guarantees higher durability. Consider a payments ledger: once a transaction is acknowledged, the user and backend must trust that the record will remain even if a data center fails. A common error is confusing durability with availability; a highly available cache might make data accessible, but without durability that data could be lost on restart. When designing durable storage, quantify recovery point objectives and note how many replicas you need and the replication guarantees (synchronous vs asynchronous). For interviews, be ready to propose durability patterns for a given consistency and availability target and explain the impact on latency and cost. Durability and Data Guarantees means durability guarantees committed data persists across failures; achieving it often requires replication and trade-offs with latency and cost.. In practical terms, ensuring committed data is not lost even under failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Durability
What durability means
Once acknowledged, data is guaranteed to survive failures and not vanish.
Techniques
  • Write-ahead logging and durable commit on disk.
  • Synchronous replication to multiple nodes or regions.
  • Periodic snapshots and immutable backups.
Trade-offs
Stronger durability increases write latency and storage costs; designers must weigh those impacts against data loss risk.
Example

A payments system writes confirmed transactions to three replicas synchronously to ensure committed data is never lost.

Checklist when designing durability
  • Define acceptable data loss (RPO).
  • Choose number of replicas and replication mode.
  • Plan recovery procedures and test them.

screens.title: Consistency and the CAP Theorem
screens.narratorSegment: Consistency in distributed systems means all clients see the same data at the same time. The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee only two of the three properties: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Partition tolerance is generally non-negotiable in real networks, so systems often trade between consistency and availability. For example, a system that must be available during network partitions may accept eventual consistency, allowing different replicas to diverge temporarily and reconcile later. Conversely, a system requiring immediate, global correctness might sacrifice availability under partitions. A common misconception is that CAP forces permanent loss of one property; rather, it guides which guarantees are available under partition conditions. In interviews, be prepared to name which two properties you choose for a scenario and explain the operational consequences. Use real examples: a banking ledger often favors consistency over availability to prevent double-spend, while a social feed may favor availability with eventual consistency to keep the service responsive. Quantify your choice: explain expected stale window or allowable downtime so the trade-off is defensible. Consistency and the CAP Theorem means because partitions happen, you must decide whether consistency or availability is the higher priority for your system and explain the trade-offs.. In practical terms, consistency, availability, and partition tolerance — pick two guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Consistency & CAP
CAP theorem — practical framing
Because network partitions occur, design choices fall between consistency and availability.
Consistency
All clients see the same data at the same time.
Availability
System answers requests even during partial failures.
Partition Tolerance
System continues operating despite network partitions.
Example: Banking
Favor consistency to avoid incorrect balances, accepting reduced availability under partitions.
Example: Social Feed
Favor availability so users keep interacting; accept eventual consistency for feeds and likes.
Interview tip

State which two properties you choose, explain the impact under partitions, and quantify the acceptable stale window or downtime to make your choice concrete.

screens.title: Quantifying NFRs — From Vague to Measurable
screens.narratorSegment: Quantifying NFRs converts wishful statements into testable targets. The process has three steps: choose the metric, choose the percentile or window, and set the acceptable objective. First, pick a metric aligned with the user experience: latency in milliseconds, throughput in requests per second, availability as percent uptime, or durability as acceptable data loss window. Second, choose how to measure distribution — percentiles are common for latency, for example 95th or 99th percentile; throughput often uses sustained requests per second. Third, set a concrete objective, such as '95 percent of requests under 100 ms' or 'handle 10,000 requests per second for peak traffic with 99.9 percent availability.' Each objective should include measurement methodology and time window. A common mistake is selecting the mean for latency; the mean can hide long tails that harm users. Use percentiles to capture tail latency. Another pitfall is not aligning metrics with business needs; always ask which metric maps to user happiness or cost impact. Finally, document how you’ll test and measure the SLO so the requirement becomes verifiable in production and during load testing. In practical terms, select metrics, choose percentiles, and set slos you can test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Finally, document how you’ll test and measure the SLO so the requirement becomes verifiable in production and during load testing. Three-step quantification
Metric → Percentile → Objective
Metric
Latency (ms), Throughput (rps), Availability (%), Durability (RPO).
Distribution
Use percentiles for latency and moving averages or sustained rates for throughput.
Objective
A concrete SLO, e.g., 99% of requests under 150 ms and 99.9% availability monthly.
Bad example
"Make the search fast" — vague, untestable.
Good example
"95% of search requests return the first page within 120 ms over a 30-day window."

screens.title: Trade-offs and Conflicts Between NFRs
screens.narratorSegment: NFRs often conflict and require strategic trade-offs. The essential skill is to name the conflict, explain why it arises, and propose a compromise with costs and benefits. Common conflicts include latency versus consistency, availability versus consistency, and durability versus latency. For example, ensuring synchronous replication for durability increases write latency, which may be unacceptable for user-facing operations. To reason through a conflict, quantify both sides: state the latency target, the desired consistency model, and the acceptable availability. Then propose architectural patterns that meet both as closely as possible: asynchronous replication with read-after-write routing, leader election with read replicas that accept eventual consistency, or hybrid models where critical data uses strong consistency and less critical data uses eventual consistency. Be explicit about the operational costs: cross-region replication costs money and increases recovery complexity. A common misconception is believing a single architecture solves all requirements — most real systems adopt mixed strategies and document which data and operations require stricter guarantees. Practice by taking a pair of NFRs, naming the trade-off, and proposing two viable architectures with pros and cons. Trade-offs and Conflicts Between NFRs means name the conflict, quantify both goals, and propose architectures that balance cost, latency, and correctness.. In practical terms, how to reason about competing goals and select practical compromises. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common conflicts and patterns
Use quantified targets to choose an architecture and document the costs.
Latency vs Consistency
Solution patterns: eventual consistency, read-your-writes via session routing, or strong consistency for critical writes only.
Durability vs Latency
Option: asynchronous replication to reduce write latency, but accept a small recovery window and compensating logic.
Availability vs Consistency
Option: favor availability with eventual consistency and background reconciliation for non-critical data.

Ride-matching: low latency for matches suggests in-memory caches and fast algorithms; strict consistency for account balances suggests strong replication and synchronous commits.

screens.title: Activity: NFR Identification for a Ride-Sharing App
screens.narratorSegment: Now apply what you’ve learned to a familiar system: a ride-sharing app. Start by writing three critical functional requirements, such as users can request rides, drivers can accept requests, and payments are processed. Next, list five critical NFRs and quantify them where possible. Propose a strategy: use local caches and regional matching for low latency while reconciling global state asynchronously to reduce cross-region coordination. Task
Complete three steps: identify functionals, list measurable NFRs, and find one NFR conflict with a proposed mitigation.
Functional requirements (examples)
  • Users can request a ride.
  • Drivers can accept and navigate to a rider.
  • The system processes payments and issues receipts.
Non-functional requirements (examples)

screens.title: Testing and Validating NFRs
screens.narratorSegment: Testing NFRs requires clear service level indicators (SLIs) and service level objectives (SLOs). An SLI is the measurement you use, such as request latency or success rate, and the SLO is the target you must meet. To validate NFRs, implement measurement instrumentation in staging and production: collect latency percentiles, error rates, throughput, and availability windows. Then run realistic load tests that mimic peak patterns and measure whether your SLOs hold. For durability, perform failure injection tests and verify no committed data is lost. For availability, run simulated instance and zone failures and confirm automated failover meets recovery objectives. A common mistake is relying solely on synthetic tests without realistic traffic shapes—tail behaviors often appear only under real-world workloads. Another pitfall is not documenting measurement windows and aggregation methods; percentiles must be computed over clear time windows to be meaningful. In an interview, describe your SLI, the percentile or aggregation you will use, the SLO target, and the test you would run to verify it. This shows you can move from requirement to measurable validation and operational readiness. Testing and Validating NFRs means define slis and slos, instrument measurement, and test with realistic failure and load scenarios to validate nfrs.. In practical terms, how to measure slis, validate slos, and test trade-offs in staging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll shift attention from what a system does to how well it does it. Functional requirements tell us the features; non-functional requirements — or NFRs — define the qualities that determine user experience, cost, and long-term success. You will learn clear definitions for scalability, availability, reliability, latency, throughput, durability, and consistency, and you will learn how to quantify them so your design decisions are testable. We’ll also examine common conflicts, like latency versus consistency, and practical trade-offs that drive architecture choices such as horizontal scaling and redundancy. Finally, you’ll practice identifying and quantifying NFRs for a real-world ride-sharing example so you can see how these abstract qualities turn into measurable targets. By the end you’ll be able to state an NFR precisely, explain its architectural implications, and propose one or two concrete design techniques to meet it. Think about a system you know; how would you describe its top quality requirement in one measurable sentence?

In this objectives overview you'll get four concrete skills to practice and prove. First, you will be able to differentiate functional and non-functional requirements with clear examples. That means when an interviewer names a requirement, you can label it and explain the architectural impact. Second, you will identify and define core NFRs such as scalability, availability, reliability, latency, throughput, and durability. You should be able to give a one-sentence definition and an example scenario for each. These two skills set your vocabulary and show you can reason about quality attributes. Third, you will explain how NFRs can conflict and require trade-offs; you should be able to pick a pair of requirements, show why they conflict, and propose an architectural compromise. Fourth, you will practice quantifying NFRs early — converting vague statements into testable targets like a 99.9% availability objective or 100 millisecond latency for 95% of requests. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a milestone you can show in interviews. Practice stating each objective as an acceptance criterion so it becomes measurable and defensible.

This screen turns objectives into interview-ready milestones and gives memory cues. For differentiating functional and non-functional, practice by naming a feature and explaining whether it describes behavior or quality, for example: 'users can upload photos' is functional; 'uploads must complete within 2 seconds' is non-functional. For identifying key NFRs, memorize six short tags: Scale, Availability, Reliability, Latency, Throughput, Durability. Attach a one-line measurable example to each tag. When explaining trade-offs, rehearse a two-sentence answer: name the conflict and propose a balancing strategy, like sacrificing global strong consistency for eventual consistency plus compensating reconciliation. For quantification, always state the metric and the percentile or SLO, for example 'latency under 100 milliseconds for 95 percent of requests.' These micro-milestones make your answers verifiable and actionable. Each objective card below includes a tiny visual mnemonic to help recall the concept and a recommended competency badge you should aim to demonstrate in an interview. Practice saying these out loud and connecting them to short architecture choices.

Start with a clear distinction: functional requirements describe what the system does — the visible behaviors and features. For example, "users can upload photos" is a functional statement. Non-functional requirements describe how well the system performs those behaviors; they are about quality attributes. An NFR could be "uploads must complete within two seconds for 95 percent of users," which constrains architecture, testing, and cost. This distinction matters because architects often select different components and trade-offs depending on quality goals. A web app that must simply store photos will emphasize correctness and durability. A photo-sharing service with millions of users must prioritize scalability and throughput. A common misconception is to think of NFRs as secondary or optional; in practice they are first-class requirements because they determine whether a feature is usable. A second misconception is treating NFRs as binary: they are measurable and continuous, so convert them into percentiles or rates. A concrete interview-ready script: name the requirement, classify it as functional or non-functional, and state its acceptance criterion. For practice, take any feature and write both a functional sentence and a measurable NFR for it. That habit forces you to design with testable goals and clear constraints.

Scalability is the system’s ability to handle increasing work by adding resources. Two common approaches are vertical scaling and horizontal scaling. Vertical scaling means making a single machine more powerful — more C P U, R A M, or disk. It’s straightforward and often cheapest early on, but it hits hard limits and creates a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads load across them. It offers higher capacity and fault tolerance, but introduces distributed complexity: state management, data partitioning, coordination, and potential consistency issues. In practice, many systems start vertical and adopt horizontal strategies as load grows. A concrete example: a small photo app might move from a beefy single database instance to a sharded cluster with read replicas as user counts rise. A common misconception is that horizontal scaling is always the better option; it often is for very large systems, but if your traffic is small, horizontal complexity is costly and unnecessary. When you choose horizontal scaling, quantify targets: number of requests per second, expected nodes, and acceptable coordination overhead. That quantification helps choose between stateless horizontal web servers, partitioned databases, or managed services that offload operational complexity.

Availability measures the proportion of time a system is accessible, usually expressed in 'nines' like 99.9% or 99.999%. Higher availability requires redundancy, automated failover, and disaster recovery plans. Reliability relates to the probability a system performs correctly over time; it captures fault tolerance and the ability to operate despite component failures. These two are related but distinct: a system can be highly available yet unreliable if it often returns incorrect or stale results. Achieving high availability often implies running redundant components across failure domains and automating detection and recovery. For reliability, design for graceful degradation and correctness under partial failures. A practical example: to achieve three nines, you might run services across two availability zones with automatic health checks and rolling restarts; to reach five nines you introduce cross-region replication and rigorous incident runbooks. A frequent misconception is equating uptime with correctness. For interviews, be prepared to propose redundancy patterns, explain failover behavior, and show how data correctness is preserved during recovery. Always quantify the target number of nines and the recovery time objective so your architectural choices can be validated.

Latency and throughput describe two different performance aspects. Latency is the time delay between a single request and its response. Low latency is critical for real-time experiences like online gaming or interactive search. Throughput measures the number of operations a system can process per unit of time, such as requests per second. A streaming service needs high throughput to serve many concurrent users. The relationship between the two can be subtle: you can have low latency for a few requests but low throughput overall, or high throughput with longer individual latencies when the system is saturated. Optimization strategies differ: to lower latency you can cache responses, optimize hot code paths, or move compute closer to the user. To increase throughput you scale horizontally, partition work, or use asynchronous processing. A frequent misconception is optimizing one while ignoring the other — for example, adding aggressive caching might reduce latency but increase staleness, impacting correctness. When designing, quantify targets like '95 percent of requests under 100 milliseconds' and 'system must sustain 10,000 requests per second' so that both dimensions are addressed with appropriate mechanisms.

Durability is the guarantee that once data is committed it will persist and not be lost, even when components fail. This is essential for databases, payment systems, and any system where loss of committed writes is unacceptable. Techniques that improve durability include write-ahead logs, synchronous replication to multiple durable stores, and stable commit protocols. There is often a cost trade-off: synchronous replication across regions increases latency and cost but guarantees higher durability. Consider a payments ledger: once a transaction is acknowledged, the user and backend must trust that the record will remain even if a data center fails. A common error is confusing durability with availability; a highly available cache might make data accessible, but without durability that data could be lost on restart. When designing durable storage, quantify recovery point objectives and note how many replicas you need and the replication guarantees (synchronous vs asynchronous). For interviews, be ready to propose durability patterns for a given consistency and availability target and explain the impact on latency and cost. Durability and Data Guarantees means durability guarantees committed data persists across failures; achieving it often requires replication and trade-offs with latency and cost.. In practical terms, ensuring committed data is not lost even under failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Consistency in distributed systems means all clients see the same data at the same time. The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee only two of the three properties: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Partition tolerance is generally non-negotiable in real networks, so systems often trade between consistency and availability. For example, a system that must be available during network partitions may accept eventual consistency, allowing different replicas to diverge temporarily and reconcile later. Conversely, a system requiring immediate, global correctness might sacrifice availability under partitions. A common misconception is that CAP forces permanent loss of one property; rather, it guides which guarantees are available under partition conditions. In interviews, be prepared to name which two properties you choose for a scenario and explain the operational consequences. Use real examples: a banking ledger often favors consistency over availability to prevent double-spend, while a social feed may favor availability with eventual consistency to keep the service responsive. Quantify your choice: explain expected stale window or allowable downtime so the trade-off is defensible. Consistency and the CAP Theorem means because partitions happen, you must decide whether consistency or availability is the higher priority for your system and explain the trade-offs.. In practical terms, consistency, availability, and partition tolerance — pick two guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Quantifying NFRs converts wishful statements into testable targets. The process has three steps: choose the metric, choose the percentile or window, and set the acceptable objective. First, pick a metric aligned with the user experience: latency in milliseconds, throughput in requests per second, availability as percent uptime, or durability as acceptable data loss window. Second, choose how to measure distribution — percentiles are common for latency, for example 95th or 99th percentile; throughput often uses sustained requests per second. Third, set a concrete objective, such as '95 percent of requests under 100 ms' or 'handle 10,000 requests per second for peak traffic with 99.9 percent availability.' Each objective should include measurement methodology and time window. A common mistake is selecting the mean for latency; the mean can hide long tails that harm users. Use percentiles to capture tail latency. Another pitfall is not aligning metrics with business needs; always ask which metric maps to user happiness or cost impact. Finally, document how you’ll test and measure the SLO so the requirement becomes verifiable in production and during load testing. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NFRs often conflict and require strategic trade-offs. The essential skill is to name the conflict, explain why it arises, and propose a compromise with costs and benefits. Common conflicts include latency versus consistency, availability versus consistency, and durability versus latency. Now apply what you’ve learned to a familiar system: a ride-sharing app. Start by writing three critical functional requirements, such as users can request rides, drivers can accept requests, and payments are processed. Next, list five critical NFRs and quantify them where possible. Example NFRs: system must handle one million concurrent ride requests during peak hours (throughput), ride-matching latency under 200 ms for 95 percent of requests (latency), availability of 99.95 percent during business hours (availability), durability so completed ride records are never lost (durability), and the system must maintain driver location updates with eventual consistency across regions (consistency). Finally, identify a conflict: for instance, ensuring extremely low latency for ride matching may conflict with strong consistency across all driver location updates. Propose a strategy: use local caches and regional matching for low latency while reconciling global state asynchronously to reduce cross-region coordination. This hybrid approach balances user experience and correctness. Practice articulating these items precisely; interviewers expect measurable NFRs and a defensible trade-off. In practical terms, practice listing functional and non-functional requirements and finding one trade-off. Testing NFRs requires clear service level indicators (SLIs) and service level objectives (SLOs). An SLI is the measurement you use, such as request latency or success rate, and the SLO is the target you must meet. To validate NFRs, implement measurement instrumentation in staging and production: collect latency percentiles, error rates, throughput, and availability windows. Then run realistic load tests that mimic peak patterns and measure whether your SLOs hold. For durability, perform failure injection tests and verify no committed data is lost. For availability, run simulated instance and zone failures and confirm automated failover meets recovery objectives. A common mistake is relying solely on synthetic tests without realistic traffic shapes—tail behaviors often appear only under real-world workloads. Another pitfall is not documenting measurement windows and aggregation methods; percentiles must be computed over clear time windows to be meaningful. In an interview, describe your SLI, the percentile or aggregation you will use, the SLO target, and the test you would run to verify it. This shows you can move from requirement to measurable validation and operational readiness. These are the core concepts you should recall quickly during a design discussion. Functional requirements define what the system does. Non-functional requirements define how well it performs and must be quantified. Scalability describes the system’s ability to increase capacity via vertical or horizontal strategies. Vertical scaling adds resources to a single machine and is simple but limited. Horizontal scaling adds machines and requires managing distributed state and consistency. Availability measures uptime as percentages or nines. Reliability measures the probability of correct operation over time. Keep these definitions short and pair them with measurable examples so you can use them in answers and justify architecture choices. If you can state one measurable target for each concept, you’ll demonstrate practical readiness rather than vague familiarity. Finish with the critical metrics and the CAP insight to carry into designs. Latency should be expressed in milliseconds with percentiles; throughput in requests per second; availability in percent uptime; and durability in terms of replication and recovery objectives. Consistency is a design decision in distributed systems and interacts directly with availability during partitions — the CAP theorem frames that choice. When you discuss a design, name the metric, state the percentile or window, and explain how your architecture meets or trades off the goal. This concise method shows you can turn vague requirements into operational targets and defend your choices with measurable validation plans.
